introduction-why-python-won-the-devops-w.core: Bash is great for piping commands on one machine. Cloud automation also needs structured data, API calls, error handling and libraries, which is where Python fits.

first_principles.problem: A Bash script that parses JSON from three cloud APIs with `grep` and `sed` breaks the first time a field moves or a value contains a space.
truths: Modern infrastructure is controlled through APIs that speak JSON.
Readable code is cheaper to maintain.
derivation: Keep Bash for **short, sequential shell glue**.
Use Python when you need **data structures, APIs, or error handling**.
Lean on its **libraries** (boto3, requests) instead of reinventing them.

analogy.title: A pocket knife vs. a workshop
analogy.story: A pocket knife is perfect for quick cuts. Building furniture needs a workbench with clamps and measured tools.
analogy.breaks: You don't have to pick one. Most ops work uses both, each where it fits.

example.title: Tag every untagged EC2 instance
example.scenario: In Bash: jq, loops and fragile quoting. In Python: a short boto3 script.

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: Readable, testable logic instead of a fragile pipeline.

example.outcome: you pick Python once the problem involves structured data or APIs.

check.q: When should you move from Bash to Python?
check.a: When the script needs structured data (JSON), API calls, real error handling or growing logic.

core-data-structures-organizing-your-inf.core: Lists keep order, dicts look things up by key, sets remove duplicates, and tuples hold fixed records. Picking the right one makes ops code both correct and simple.

first_principles.problem: Storing servers in a list and then searching it for one by name gets slow and messy. Sets and dicts solve that directly.
truths: Different questions need different access patterns.
Dict and set lookups are O(1).
Immutable data can't be changed by accident.

analogy.title: Storage in a workshop
analogy.story: A queue of jobs (list), labelled drawers (dict), a guest list with no duplicates (set), a sealed parts kit (tuple).
analogy.breaks: Real data often nests: a list of dicts is the typical shape of an API response.

example.title: Find hosts missing from monitoring
example.scenario: Compare the inventory with the monitored hosts.

steps.label: Why a set
steps.detail: A set difference does in one line what nested loops would otherwise need.

example.outcome: the data structure answers the question directly.

check.q: Which structure suits 'is this IP in the blocklist?'
check.a: A set, because membership checks are O(1).

dependency-isolation-venv-and-pip.core: Each project gets its own virtual environment with pinned package versions, so one project's upgrade can't break another and every machine installs the same thing.

first_principles.problem: A script works with boto3 1.26 on your laptop but crashes on a colleague's machine with a globally installed 1.34.
truths: Packages change their APIs between versions.
A global install is shared by every project.
derivation: **Pin** versions in requirements.txt or a lock file.
Never `sudo pip install` into the system Python.

analogy.title: A separate toolbox per job
analogy.story: Each job has its own toolbox, so lending a wrench out of one doesn't leave another job without it.
analogy.breaks: A venv isolates Python packages, not system libraries. For those you need containers.

example.title: Onboarding a new teammate
example.scenario: They clone the repo and run three commands.

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: They get the same versions you have.

code.text:
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

example.outcome: the script behaves the same on every machine.

check.a: Every project shares them, so upgrading for one project can break another.

mastering-http-with-requests.core: Production API calls need session reuse, timeouts and retries with backoff. Without them a slow or flaky endpoint can hang or crash your automation.

first_principles.problem: `requests.get(url)` with no timeout can hang forever, and one transient 503 can kill a long-running job.
truths: A call with no timeout can wait forever.
Opening a fresh connection for every call is slow.

analogy.title: Calling a busy helpdesk
analogy.story: Stay on one call (session), hang up after a while (timeout), and call back later, waiting longer each time (backoff).
analogy.breaks: Only retry idempotent requests. Retrying a POST can create duplicates.

example.title: Polling a status API
example.scenario: A session with a retry adapter and a timeout.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: A transient 503 is retried quietly and a dead host fails within 5 seconds.

code.text:
s = requests.Session()
s.mount("https://", HTTPAdapter(max_retries=Retry(total=5, backoff_factor=1, status_forcelist=[429, 502, 503])))
r = s.get(url, timeout=5)
r.raise_for_status()

example.outcome: the automation survives normal network flakiness.

check.a: Without one, a stalled server can block the script forever.

automating-aws-with-boto3-paginators-and.core: AWS returns large lists one page at a time, and many operations finish asynchronously. Paginators fetch every page for you; waiters poll until a resource reaches the state you want.

first_principles.problem: A script that lists S3 objects silently stops at 1,000. Another script tries to use an instance that is still 'pending'.
truths: APIs cap how many results one response returns.
derivation: Use **get_paginator()** so you get every result.
Use **get_waiter()** to block until the resource is ready.
Let boto3 handle the tokens and polling intervals.

analogy.title: Reading a multi-page report and waiting for a kettle
analogy.story: You turn every page, not just the first. You wait for the kettle to click instead of lifting the lid every second.
analogy.breaks: Waiters have a maximum wait, so a resource that is truly stuck still produces an error you must handle.

example.title: Launch an instance and list every bucket object

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: No missing objects and no race with a pending instance.

example.outcome: the script handles both scale and asynchrony correctly.

check.q: Why might a list call return only 1,000 items?
check.a: The API pages its results. Without a paginator you only read the first page.

log-analysis-basics-with-pandas.core: pandas loads logs into a table, so filtering, grouping and counting become one-line queries, and malformed lines are easy to deal with.

first_principles.problem: Shell pipelines like `grep | awk | sort | uniq -c` break on irregular log lines, and they struggle with multi-column questions.
truths: Logs are structured rows that happen to be written as text.
Most ops questions are 'group by X, count or average Y'.
A table is easier to query than a stream.
derivation: Sort and take the top N.

analogy.title: A spreadsheet instead of a notepad
analogy.story: Once the rows are in columns, sorting and pivoting take one click.
analogy.breaks: pandas loads everything into memory, so huge logs need chunking or a real log platform.

example.title: Top error-producing IPs
example.scenario: Parse the access log and count 5xx responses per IP.

steps.label: Answer
steps.detail: The five noisiest IPs, in two lines.

example.outcome: ad-hoc log questions take seconds to answer.

check.q: What pandas operation answers 'errors per server'?
check.a: Filter to error rows, then groupby server and count (or value_counts).
